seed.text: Play Isn't Proper in Cemetery, Including People and Dogs

prompt: I volunteer with a small cemetery that used to be attached to a church but is now maintained by the town. Since new apartments went up nearby, people have started cutting through it: parents let children run between the stones, teenagers toss a ball on the open grass, and dog walkers use the paths. Last week a dog lifted its leg near a veteran’s marker during a family’s anniversary prayers. The new cemetery superintendent says the town has adopted clear rules: open from dawn to dusk, leashed dogs allowed, quiet recreation allowed, no alcohol, no climbing on markers, no disturbing services. He told volunteers not to scold visitors if they are following the posted rules. Some older families want signs saying “No dogs, no games—this is hallowed ground” before Memorial Day. I’ve been asked to speak at the next cemetery board meeting.

responses.Purity: I would speak for the signs. A cemetery is not just spare green space the town happens to maintain; it is a place set apart for the dead, for mourning, and for prayer. Running games and dogs relieving themselves near graves make the whole place feel profaned, even if no one means insult. The stones are not scenery. They mark bodies, vows, names, sacrifices, and family rites that deserve quiet. If the posted rules allow people to treat consecrated ground like a pocket park, then the rules are wrong and should be changed. I would be respectful to the superintendent, but I would not pretend his permission makes it proper. Ask for a clear boundary: walking through is one thing; playing and bringing dogs among graves crosses a line.
responses.Authority: I would tell the board to follow the superintendent’s rules unless and until they are formally changed. He is the official charged with maintaining the cemetery, balancing public access, and setting enforceable standards. Volunteers should not create their own code at the gate because they feel strongly; that leads to arguments, selective scolding, and confusion for visitors who are obeying the posted policy. The right path is to bring concerns to the board, hear from residents and families, and vote on any revisions. Until then, a leashed dog on a path or a child quietly playing on open grass is permitted. Respect for the place also means respecting the people entrusted to govern it. If every family’s personal sense of what is improper overrides the rules, the cemetery becomes harder to manage and less orderly.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I’m helping run a community gallery night where every contributor has always received the same public acknowledgment: their name on the entrance board, a mention from the host, and a page in the keepsake booklet. This year, Mateo submitted a piece about shame and the body. It includes clean but intentionally “soiled-looking” sheets, recordings of bathroom sounds, and a cracked replica of a saint figure placed in a laundry basket. The venue has cleared it as safe, and Mateo followed the submission rules. Several older volunteers say the work is degrading, especially the treatment of the saint image, and they do not want his name honored alongside everyone else’s during the opening remarks. I have to finalize the program tonight.

responses.Equality: Put Mateo in the program and read his name like everyone else’s. The whole point of a shared community event is that recognition is not handed out only to people whose taste, religion, or manners match the committee’s. He submitted within the rules, took part in the work, and belongs on the same list as the watercolor painters and quilt makers. If people dislike the piece, they can say so, skip that room, or write a response. But once we start withholding basic acknowledgment because some contributors are seen as embarrassing or tainted, the event stops being a common space and becomes a club controlled by whoever can claim the cleanest sensibilities. Equal public credit is not a medal for purity; it is the minimum sign that each participant counts.
responses.Purity: I would not give that piece the same public honor during the opening. This is not about silencing Mateo as a person; it is about refusing to treat deliberate defilement as just another contribution to celebrate. A saint image, even a replica, is not a prop to be cracked and tossed into a laundry basket for shock. Pairing it with staged filth and bathroom sounds makes the whole room feel debased. A community gallery can be open without blessing every gesture with ceremony and applause. Let the work stand if the rules require it, but do not ask the host to speak his name in the same honoring tone as those who offered beauty, craft, or remembrance. Public recognition should not wash away the difference between expression and degradation.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: After a wildfire, the town asks Leila to organize a public thank-you gathering for everyone who kept the evacuation center running. The list includes incident commanders, firefighters, nurses, radio operators, cooks, cleaners, drivers, and teenagers who folded blankets after school. Leila wants name tags with no titles, mixed seating, and one shared roll call where each person is asked to stand for the same applause. Several senior responders object. They say the program should mark who worked through the worst nights, who made life-or-death calls, and who only helped briefly. They want longer introductions for the people who carried the heaviest load and separate seats near the front for those with major responsibilities. Leila has to send the final program tonight.

responses.Equality: I would keep the gathering arranged so everyone is met with the same public respect. In a crisis, rank can easily turn into a signal that some people matter more as human beings. The cleaner who kept the bathrooms usable, the teenager stacking blankets, and the commander making decisions were all part of keeping frightened neighbors safe. Different tasks are not different levels of dignity. If you put certain titles at the front and give them grander introductions, the message to the quieter workers is that their presence is decorative. You can thank people sincerely without building a staircase of importance in the room. Let the record elsewhere describe specific duties if needed. This gathering should say: when our town depended on people, no one’s standing was beneath anyone else’s.
responses.Proportionality: I would not flatten the program. Respecting everyone does not mean pretending everyone carried the same burden. Some people trained for years, stayed awake through the worst hours, took responsibility when mistakes could have been disastrous, and kept working while others helped for a short shift. If the ceremony gives identical recognition to all of them, it becomes less honest, not more respectful. People deserve to have their actual contribution seen. The cook and the cleaner should absolutely be thanked, but the firefighter who entered dangerous areas or the coordinator who made the hardest calls should be named for that. Clear distinctions are not insults; they are a way of telling the truth about effort, responsibility, and sacrifice. A community should honor every helper while still recognizing who gave and risked the most.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: After a flash flood, Maple Grove High managed to evacuate students quickly. The superintendent is planning a public thank-you ceremony. Principal Alvarez wants the stage to include custodians, bus drivers, cafeteria workers, aides, teachers, and administrators in identical seats, with the same speaking time and the same title in the program: “Evacuation Team.” A few staff object. They say the assistant principals and two teachers designed the plan, trained others, and made the hardest calls during the emergency, while some employees simply followed instructions for a few minutes. They want the program to distinguish levels of responsibility and give longer remarks to those who carried the heaviest load. Alvarez worries that the ceremony will quietly teach students that some kinds of work make people more worthy of being heard.

responses.Equality: I would keep the stage and speaking time the same. A school is full of invisible status lines already: who has an office, who gets called “professional,” whose work is treated as background. In a crisis, students saw adults depend on each other. The bus driver who kept children calm and the custodian who opened the right hallway are not lesser people because their job titles are lower. A public ceremony is not a technical report; it tells the community who counts. If we separate everyone into tiers, the old hierarchy will swallow the lesson. You can describe what happened in the narrative, but don’t arrange bodies on stage as if dignity has ranks. Let every member of the team sit in the same kind of chair, use the same title, and speak as someone whose presence mattered.
responses.Proportionality: I would acknowledge everyone respectfully, but the ceremony should not pretend the contributions were the same. Respecting people does not require flattening real differences in responsibility, preparation, and judgment. If two teachers spent months building the plan and administrators had to make decisions under pressure, they earned more space to explain their work. That is not saying a custodian or bus driver is worth less as a person; it is saying credit should track what people actually did. Students also need to learn that effort and responsibility matter. When recognition is identical no matter the load carried, it can feel dishonest to the people who sacrificed more and confusing to those watching. Give everyone a place in the program, name each role clearly, but let the main remarks and special acknowledgment go to those whose contribution was greatest.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At a neighborhood disaster-preparedness group in Quezon City, volunteers spent three months creating an evacuation plan. Some, like Marisol and Jun, attended every mapping session, checked routes in the rain, and trained block captains. Others came only once or twice but still live in the area and will be affected by the plan. At the final meeting, the group must choose which routes become official and who speaks for the neighborhood at the city hearing. Marisol proposes that every resident present get the same speaking time and one vote, because the plan will govern everyone’s safety and daily life. Jun argues that people who did the hard work and know the details should have more time to explain and more weight in the final decision. The chair asks for advice before setting the meeting rules.

responses.Equality: Give every resident in the room the same chance to speak and the same vote. This plan will shape what happens to all of them in an emergency, not just to the people who had flexible schedules or the confidence to join every session. Someone who attended once may know about an elderly neighbor, a blocked alley, or a child-care problem that the regular volunteers missed. If the meeting privileges the most active members, it turns a community decision into an insiders’ decision. Marisol and Jun can present what they learned, and people will naturally take their expertise seriously. But the rules should not make some residents count more as residents. The group needs trust when the sirens go off, and trust starts with everyone knowing their voice had the same standing.
responses.Proportionality: Jun is right to ask that the people who did the work have more room to guide the decision. This is not a casual opinion poll; it is a technical plan built from months of route checks, training sessions, and hard conversations with block captains. If someone came once, they should absolutely be heard, but their judgment should not carry the same weight as someone who knows why a certain alley was rejected or which route floods first. Giving identical speaking time can reward absence and bury hard-earned knowledge under last-minute impressions. Let every resident raise concerns, then let the committed volunteers explain, answer, and make the final recommendation. People who carried the responsibility should not be treated as interchangeable with people who mostly stayed away.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I’m on the steering group for New Dawn House, a community space with an ancestor wall, a shared kitchen, and a hall used for language classes, memorial meals, dance nights, and meetings. A small “clean table” circle has always arranged the annual remembrance supper. This year they said two newer members may attend but should not light candles, choose music, or speak during the opening because they have publicly performed in erotic art and, in the circle’s words, “treat the body like a prop.” They also want continuing veto power over decorations and performances in the hall so the house does not become “vulgar.” Other members say no inner circle should be able to rank everyone’s dignity or control a space that belongs to the whole community.

responses.Equality: I would not let that circle keep veto power or decide who is fit to speak. New Dawn House is a shared community, not a private shrine run by a few self-appointed gatekeepers. If someone is a member in good standing, they should have the same standing at meetings, the same chance to lead, and the same voice in what happens in the hall. Once you accept the idea that one faction can mark others as lesser, you have already changed the house into a hierarchy. People can personally dislike a performance or decline to take part in a ritual with someone, but they should not get special control over everyone else’s roles. Set clear, common rules for the space, rotate responsibilities, and let the whole membership decide together.
responses.Purity: I would protect the remembrance supper and the ancestor wall from being treated like just another activity room. The circle may sound severe, but they are trying to preserve a boundary that gives the house its meaning. Some acts make a space feel debased, even if no one is injured. When people publicly turn intimacy and the body into spectacle, it is reasonable to say they should not light the candles or set the tone for a sacred meal of remembrance. That is not about hating them or expelling them; they can still attend, learn, and belong. But belonging does not require making every role interchangeable. A community that cannot say “this is clean enough for our dead, and that is not” will eventually lose the very reverence it was built to carry.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt:
Leila coordinates a community language circle that meets at a public library. There are three small rooms: one quiet room with a window and whiteboard, one cramped room near the children’s area, and one open table in the noisy lobby. Everyone prefers the quiet room, especially people leading beginner sessions.

For the last six months, a core group has prepared lessons, welcomed newcomers, and stayed late to put materials away. Several newer members attend only when convenient and rarely help. Now the schedule for the next term has to be posted. The core group says the quiet room should go first to people who have carried the circle and proved they will use it well. Others say every facilitator should rotate through the best room, including irregular volunteers, because the circle belongs equally to all who show up to teach.

responses.Equality: Rotate the quiet room. If the circle starts treating the best space as something people have to earn, the newer and less confident facilitators will always be stuck on the margins. That changes the spirit of the group. Everyone who is trusted to lead a session should have the same standing when rooms are assigned. The people who have helped for months deserve thanks and public appreciation, but not permanent first claim on the good conditions. A rotation also prevents a small inner circle from quietly becoming the owners of a shared project. If someone signs up and then fails to show up, handle that specific problem. But don’t assume the most established people are naturally entitled to the best room. Give everyone a fair turn, posted in advance, so no one has to beg for access.
responses.Proportionality: Give the quiet room first to the people who have carried the work. That is not favoritism; it is recognizing responsibility. The best room helps the session run smoothly, and the people who prepare, welcome newcomers, and clean up have shown they will use it seriously. If someone rarely helps and only appears when it suits them, they should not have the same claim as someone who has kept the circle alive week after week. Equal rotation sounds fair, but it ignores effort and reliability. It can also discourage the dependable volunteers, because it tells them their extra work makes no difference. Let newer facilitators earn earlier access by taking on tasks and showing consistency. The path should be open, but the order should reflect contribution.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I’m on the conduct panel at a small religious college. During a late-night rehearsal in the chapel, Naveen posed for a photo pretending to use the baptismal font as a sink for his muddy hands. He did not actually put his hands in the water, but he leaned over it, made a face, and posted the picture with a crude caption. Students who saw it were upset; a few said the chapel now feels defiled. Naveen apologized, deleted the post, and said he was showing off, not attacking anyone’s faith. His record is clean. The chaplain wants him barred from chapel roles for the rest of the year and excluded from the upcoming ceremony. Others on the panel think a formal apology and a short loss of leadership duties would fit what he actually did.

responses.Proportionality: What Naveen did was disrespectful, and he should feel the weight of that. But the consequence has to match the act, not the worst feeling people have about it. He didn’t damage the font, contaminate the water, interrupt worship, or target a person. He staged an ugly joke and posted it. That calls for a real correction: a public apology to the chapel community, a meeting with the chaplain, and losing leadership duties for a limited time. If we treat a foolish photo like a grave desecration, we stop distinguishing between immaturity and malice. A clean record and a sincere apology should matter. Discipline should teach him and reassure others that the chapel is respected, not mark him as if he committed something far more serious than he did.
responses.Purity: I would not treat this as just a rude post. A baptismal font is not a prop, and muddy hands near it with a crude caption makes a sacred place feel dirty. Even if the water was not touched, he used the image of contamination to get a laugh. That is exactly why people feel the chapel has been degraded. Someone who does that should not be standing in chapel roles a few weeks later as though the space can simply absorb the insult. Excluding him from the ceremony and from chapel roles for the year is not revenge; it is a way of restoring the boundary around what is holy. His apology can be sincere and still not make him ready to represent that space. Some things require distance, cleansing, and time before trust should return.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: Leila is president of a university climbing club. The Saturday trips to the scenic outdoor crags have limited van seats and everyone wants them, especially the beginner-friendly ones with experienced belayers. For years, the board has let trip leaders, gear checkers, route planners, and members who attend safety workshops sign up first. Newer members say the same tight circle keeps getting the best outings, while casual members only see leftover spots. They want a rotation or lottery so every member gets a fair chance at the good trips, not just the people with the most time to help run the club. Several veteran members warn that if effort no longer affects access, fewer people will do the unglamorous safety and planning work. Leila has to set the sign-up rule before Friday.

responses.Equality: I would move to a rotation or lottery for the most desirable trips. A club should not become a place where the same insiders always get first claim on the best experiences. Some people have class schedules, family duties, anxiety about volunteering, or simply joined later; that should not mean they are permanently stuck at the back of the line. If these trips are part of belonging to the club, everyone should have a real turn, not just a theoretical chance after the regulars finish choosing. You can still ask trained members to staff each trip, and you can schedule separate appreciation for the people who help. But access to the club’s best opportunities should circulate. Otherwise the message to newcomers is clear: this is our group, and you get what we leave behind.
responses.Proportionality: I would keep priority for the people who do the work that makes the trips possible. Those seats are not just a treat; they are connected to hours spent checking harnesses, planning routes, attending safety sessions, and taking responsibility for beginners on the rock. If someone gives up time and effort so the club can function, it is fair that they have first access to the outings they helped create. A pure lottery treats the member who shows up only for fun exactly like the member who makes sure everyone gets home safely. That will breed resentment among the dependable people and eventually weaken the club. New members should absolutely have a path in: attend trainings, help with gear, shadow trip leaders, then get priority too. But benefits should follow contribution, not ignore it.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: The volunteer fire brigade in Port Alia has always let its captain assign training partners, speaking time in meetings, and who represents the brigade at town safety events. Captain Morales has served for thirty years, knows every procedure, and was chosen under the brigade’s bylaws. Lately, newer members say his inner circle gets the visible roles and that objections are cut off with “I’ve earned the right to decide.” They want meeting agendas set by rotating members, open discussion before assignments, and term limits for captain. Older firefighters warn that emergency work depends on clear rank, not people treating the brigade like a debating club. At next week’s meeting, Aisha must decide whether to support the reform proposal.

responses.Equality: Aisha should support the reform. A captain can coordinate an emergency without owning the whole brigade. When the same person and his close friends control who speaks, who is seen, and who gets trusted roles, the rest become passengers in an organization they help sustain. That breeds silence, resentment, and blind spots. Rotating agenda control and letting members challenge assignments does not mean chaos; it means no one’s voice is treated as naturally above everyone else’s outside the moment of command. If Captain Morales is as capable as people say, his reasons can stand in the open. Term limits are not an insult to his service. They are a safeguard against any one circle becoming permanent rulers of a group that belongs to all its members.
responses.Authority: Aisha should not back a proposal that weakens the captain’s office. A fire brigade is not a book club. Its habits in ordinary meetings shape how people respond when orders matter, and members must know that rank is real. Captain Morales was selected under the rules, has decades of experience, and carries responsibility when things go wrong. Newer members may dislike some assignments, but that does not mean they understand what the captain is seeing about readiness, judgment, and temperament. Open discussion is fine when invited, yet turning agendas and leadership terms into a contest will make every decision feel provisional. If there are concerns, they should be brought respectfully through existing channels. Undermining the recognized captain to prove no one stands above anyone else is dangerous for this kind of institution.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At a neighborhood makerspace, the two evening laser-cutter slots are the only times most members can use the machine. A small group of certified members also spends extra hours cleaning the cutter, teaching safety checks, replacing worn parts, and staying late when someone’s project jams. They have informally taken first claim on the evening slots, saying the shop would not run without them. Newer certified members complain that they almost never get a convenient turn and that the same familiar faces control the best access. Samira, the volunteer coordinator, has to write a clear sign-up rule before the next calendar opens. What should she recommend?

responses.Equality: Rotate the prime slots. The evening access belongs to the whole makerspace, not to the people who already have the strongest position inside it. I respect the members who clean, teach, and fix problems, and they deserve public thanks and real appreciation. But if extra service becomes the gateway to decent hours, then people with more free time, more confidence, or longer-standing friendships will keep getting the best opportunities. New members will stay outsiders because they cannot get enough convenient access to become regular contributors themselves. A fair calendar should make sure everyone certified gets a real turn, including the quiet person who follows the rules but cannot hang around all week. Recognize service separately; do not let it turn into control over a shared resource.
responses.Proportionality: Give first claim to the members who keep the shop functioning. Those evening slots are valuable because someone cleaned the lens, checked the ventilation, trained beginners, and handled jams instead of walking away. Treating the person who only appears for a convenient slot exactly the same as the person who makes the machine usable sends the wrong message. It encourages taking without carrying any of the load. Priority does not have to mean a closed club: make the criteria clear, rotate among active contributors, and leave later openings for everyone certified. But the best access should reflect real contribution and reliability. If people want the most convenient turns, they can join the maintenance roster, mentor newcomers, or help with safety checks. Privileges should follow what people put into the place.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: The neighborhood garden committee is choosing which plots will become a children’s area, a compost station, and a quiet seating space. Priya joined two months ago and has attended every open meeting. A few longtime volunteers, including Mateo, spent years clearing weeds, building paths, and keeping the garden alive when almost no one came. At the final meeting, Priya asks that every member get the same speaking time and one vote. Mateo argues that people who have done most of the work should get longer to speak and more influence over the layout, because they understand the garden and earned that trust through effort.

responses.Equality: Give everyone the same speaking time and one vote. A shared committee is not a private club for the people who arrived first or worked the most hours. Priya is a member now, and the children, neighbors, and newer gardeners will live with the decision too. If longtime volunteers can turn past effort into extra voice, then newcomers are always guests, never equals, no matter how faithfully they show up. That is how groups become closed circles where the same people keep shaping everything. Mateo’s work deserves thanks, and people should listen carefully to his experience, but listening is not the same as giving him more power. The fairest meeting is one where every person can stand on the same ground, speak without being crowded out, and cast a vote that counts exactly as much as anyone else’s.
responses.Proportionality: Mateo and the other longtime volunteers should have more weight in this decision. That is not because Priya is unwelcome; it is because responsibility and sacrifice should matter. The people who cleared the weeds, repaired the paths, and kept the garden going through bad seasons have shown commitment in a way that occasional or new members simply have not yet had the chance to show. They also know which spaces flood, where children actually gather, and what maintenance each idea will require. Giving identical influence to someone who just arrived treats effort as if it counts for nothing. Priya should be heard respectfully, but final influence should track contribution and knowledge. Otherwise the committee teaches that you can step in at the end and shape what others built, with the same authority as the people who carried it for years.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt:
At the Southside Heritage Center, a dozen volunteers spent months building an exhibit about family rituals. The usual practice is to put every volunteer’s name in the same size on the entrance wall, whether someone sorted one box of photos or designed half the rooms.

Near the end, Leila added a small performance piece without asking first. She wore an old white ceremonial shawl from the storage collection and used it in a scene meant to criticize “fear of the body.” Nothing was damaged; the shawl was cleaned and returned. Still, several elders said she had made a sacred garment feel defiled, turning something meant for prayer and mourning into a prop for bodily display.

Now the wall text is being finalized. The director asks whether Leila’s name should appear with the other volunteers’ names.

responses.Equality: Put Leila’s name on the wall with everyone else’s. The credit line is not a purity test or a ceremony of approval; it is a record of who helped make the exhibit. Once we start deciding that some contributors deserve full visibility and others deserve erasure because their taste or symbolism offended people, the equal standing of the group disappears. The person who sorted one folder, the person who painted labels, and the person whose idea upset the elders all took part in the work. If the center needs clearer rules about sacred objects, make them and apply them going forward. If it wants to add a note explaining that the performance was disputed, do that honestly. But do not single out Leila by making her the only volunteer whose labor becomes invisible.
responses.Purity: I would not put Leila’s name in the same honored place as the others. That wall is not just an inventory of tasks; it is the center publicly saying, “These are the people we thank for carrying this heritage well.” She took a garment set aside for prayer and mourning and used it for bodily provocation. Even if it was later cleaned, the meaning of the act matters. Some things are kept apart because they carry dignity, grief, and sacred memory. Treating them as raw material for self-expression lowers the whole exhibit. She can be told privately that her time is known, and the center can keep an internal record. But public recognition should not pretend that defiling a sacred object is just another contribution beside careful stewardship.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: The campus radio station has one slot everyone wants: Friday evening, when the most students listen and bands often stop by. For the past year, Lina and Mateo have hosted it because they rebuilt the music archive, trained new DJs, and cover late-night gaps when others cancel. Now several newer members say the station is starting to feel like a private club. They point to the charter, which says the best airtime should circulate so every member gets a real chance to learn, be heard, and shape the station’s sound. At Sunday’s meeting, the station manager has to decide whether to keep the Friday slot with the two most proven hosts or put it into a rotation that includes everyone who has completed basic training.

responses.Equality: Put the Friday slot into a real rotation. A student station should not become a place where the same reliable people keep the best chances indefinitely while everyone else waits on the edge. Lina and Mateo deserve thanks, but gratitude should not turn into ownership. New DJs cannot prove themselves in meaningful ways if the meaningful opportunities are already locked up. If someone has completed the training and agrees to the standards, they should get a turn at the slot that actually matters. You can still ask experienced hosts to mentor, help with handoffs, or step in when someone is absent. But the message should be clear: this station belongs to all its members, not just the people who arrived earlier or have the strongest reputation.
responses.Proportionality: Keep the Friday slot with Lina and Mateo, or at least give it only to people who have shown the same level of commitment. That slot matters because listeners count on it, visiting bands count on it, and the station’s reputation is tied to it. Lina and Mateo did not simply claim a privilege; they earned trust by doing the unglamorous work, showing up when others did not, and making the station better for everyone. Handing the best slot to people who have only completed basic training treats steady service and casual participation as if they are the same. They are not. New members should absolutely have paths to grow: guest segments, substitute nights, co-hosting, and clear benchmarks. But access to the most visible role should follow demonstrated responsibility, not just membership.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I help run a community dance festival where the ancestral masks are kept in a locked dressing room. The written rule says that anyone who plays with a mask outside rehearsal loses their performance role for the next event; last year, a quiet younger dancer got exactly that consequence for joking around with one. This week, Leila, the troupe captain and the person everyone expects to lead the opening procession, filmed herself wearing the oldest mask in a bathroom mirror and making a mocking face. Elders are upset that the mask was taken into an unclean place and treated like a joke. Some performers say Leila is too important to remove; others say the mask and the ceremony have been defiled. The festival committee meets tonight to decide Leila’s place in the opening procession.

responses.Equality: Apply the rule exactly as it is written. Leila should lose her performance role for the next event, just as the younger dancer did last year. Her being captain, talented, or popular should not make the rule softer; the elders’ anger and the mask’s importance should not make the rule suddenly harsher either. People need to know that rules mean the same thing when the person in trouble has friends, status, or a central role. If the committee now invents a special consequence, everyone will wonder whether discipline depends on who caused the outrage rather than what the rule says. Clean and repair the mask however the elders think is proper, and revise the rule for future cases if it is too weak. But Leila’s consequence should match the rule everyone else has been held to.
responses.Purity: Leila should not lead the opening procession. This is not just “playing with a mask.” She took the oldest ancestral mask into a bathroom, wore it for a mocking image, and treated something sacred as a costume gag. A ceremony cannot simply continue as if that stain is no different from ordinary clowning around in rehearsal. Until the mask is properly cleansed and Leila has made a serious apology to the elders and the troupe, putting her at the front would make the whole procession feel cheap and contaminated. I would say the same if she were the least popular dancer. Some things carry a sanctity that rules on a page may fail to protect. When someone drags a sacred object into an unclean setting, the response has to restore reverence, not merely check a disciplinary box.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: Maya belongs to an eight-person neighborhood group preparing testimony about a proposed bus-lane redesign. responses.Proportionality: I would tell Maya that influence here should follow real contribution. Everyone can be treated respectfully and allowed to offer comments, but the public message should be shaped mainly by those who did the work and know the evidence. Otherwise the group rewards showing up at the end and overruling months of effort. That breeds resentment and makes serious volunteers wonder why they bothered. I’d give each member a brief chance to speak internally, but weight the final vote and the hearing time toward the people who contributed most to producing the testimony.

Afterward, the team can confront him hard, make him apologize, and decide what place he has going forward. But a captain should not abandon her own people at the moment they most need protection.

author: gpt-5.5

author: gpt-5.5

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: After a citywide power outage, the recreation center hosted a review meeting for everyone who helped: emergency managers, volunteer drivers, janitors, nurses, translators, and teenagers who checked on elderly neighbors. author: gpt-5.5

author: gpt-5.5
prompt:

responses.Equality: I would push for the changes, respectfully but firmly. A council is not supposed to become one person’s court, with everyone else waiting for permission to matter. The title may let Mateo organize meetings, but it does not make his friends more important than the rest of you or give them permanent control over whose voices are heard. If younger members are always interrupted and the same people always get visibility, then the council is no longer representing the students. responses.Authority: I would be careful about turning this into a challenge to the office itself. The handbook gives the head prefect responsibility to direct the council and represent it, and that role exists for a reason. Schools need lines of responsibility, especially in bodies that speak to administrators and the wider student body. If every decision about procedure becomes a contest, the council can quickly lose discipline and credibility. That does not mean Mateo should be rude or favoritistic. I would advise you to request a formal meeting with him and the faculty advisor, cite specific examples, and ask him to use his authority more fairly. author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At Saffron House, twelve residents share one kitchen and take turns leading the weekly communal supper. responses.Equality: Rhea should not accept a Clean Kitchen Circle with special rank over everyone else. responses.Purity: I would support the Clean Kitchen Circle. The kitchen is not just a neutral room with appliances; it is where the house gathers, prepares food, and shares a table. If dead flesh and egg residue are kept beside the common dishes, many residents experience the whole place as stained, even if someone insists it has been scrubbed. That feeling is not a whim. Some things degrade a shared space by being brought into it. People who do not care about that should not be the ones deciding how clean the kitchen may remain. The circle is trying to protect the room from becoming anything-goes. Residents can eat what they want elsewhere, but the main kitchen and table should be kept free of what makes them feel polluted.

author: gpt-5.5

responses.Equality: I would keep the alphabetical author list and give everyone a real speaking part. author: gpt-5.5

responses.Care: I would give Amira the featured line. Not because the others do not matter, but because this moment could genuinely help a hurt young person feel less alone. author: gpt-5.5
prompt: The neighborhood language club has grown from twelve people in a church basement to more than a hundred members. Meena and the original volunteers built the lesson plans, trained tutors, opened and closed the rooms, and have attended almost every session for years. Now the club is voting on whether to change its meeting format and choose a new coordinator. responses.Equality: Give every member the same speaking time and the same vote. The whole point of a club like this is that no one stands above the others once they are part of it. Meena and the early volunteers deserve thanks, public recognition, and trust, but not a louder voice built into the rules. If newcomers know their say counts less, they will never feel like full members; they will feel like guests in someone else’s project. That is how informal ownership turns into control. Let Meena speak as persuasively as she can within the same limits as everyone else. Her experience will carry weight naturally, because people will listen to it. But the final decision should come from members meeting one another as equals, not from a ranking of whose time in the club makes their voice worth more.
responses.Proportionality: Meena is right to ask for extra weight for the people who have actually sustained the club. A vote about its future is not the same as a casual preference poll. The members who designed the lessons, trained tutors, solved problems, and showed up for years have earned deeper authority over decisions that could undo their work. Giving the same formal say to someone who joined last month and someone who carried the club through difficult years treats unequal contributions as if they were identical. That is not respectful; it is careless. New members should be welcomed and heard, but major choices should lean toward those who have demonstrated commitment. Longer speaking time for experienced volunteers is sensible because they know the history and consequences. Extra voting weight is not a privilege grabbed from others; it is recognition of responsibility already proven.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt:

responses.Equality: Apply the handbook rule exactly. responses.Purity: This cannot be treated like an ordinary misuse of a room. A chapel is not just campus space with a reservation calendar; it is a place people enter with reverence, grief, prayer, and trust. She should step away from commencement and from chapel events until she has made a sincere apology and the space has been ritually restored in whatever way the chaplaincy finds appropriate. author: gpt-5.5
prompt:

responses.Equality: You should support the changes. Gratitude for what those families did does not give them the right to keep everyone else underneath them. A community association belongs to the whole community, not to the people who happened to arrive first or endured the hardest years. If newer members can only nod along while one circle controls the stage, the seats, the stories, and the agenda, then participation is mostly symbolic. Rotating chairs and open nominations are not insults; they are basic safeguards against one group becoming permanent rulers. responses.Loyalty: I would be very careful about joining a push that makes the founding families feel cast aside. When the group was vulnerable, they were the ones who stood together and took the heat. That kind of loyalty creates obligations. A community is not just a procedure where every person who walks in gets to rearrange it immediately. The newer members are enjoying a space that exists because those families protected it. If you force term limits and open challenges right before the festival, it will look like betrayal, not reform, and people may stop trusting one another. Start by backing the founders publicly and asking them to bring others in gradually. They deserve to feel that their own community still stands with them.

responses.Purity: I would leave his name off that ceremonial cloth. This is not just a volunteer roster pinned to a noticeboard; it is part of a rededication in a sacred room. Carrying his name into the chapel with candles and prayers would tell the elders that the insult does not matter as long as he also did useful work. author: gpt-5.5

responses.Authority: In a flood response, the chain of command is not a decoration; it is what keeps a hard situation from becoming chaos. author: gpt-5.5

responses.Proportionality: I would not put Mateo and Priya on the main curator panel or give them equal speaking time. That is not cruelty; it is honesty. Public credit should tell the truth about who carried the work. If someone can disappear, ignore the team, and then stand beside the people who did the scanning, captioning, interviews, and repairs, you teach everyone that effort means nothing. The reliable volunteers are not being petty for wanting the record to reflect reality. I would acknowledge Mateo and Priya for the specific pieces they actually helped with, if any, and invite them to contribute more next time. But the central roles and recognition belong to the people who showed up. Sharing those honors equally would be taking from the workers and handing it to the coasters.
responses.Equality: I would keep Mateo and Priya listed with the group and allow them the same brief speaking slot as the others. The center’s rule matters precisely when people are frustrated. Once we start sorting volunteers into “real” members and “lesser” members, the project becomes another place where status is guarded and people are publicly shamed. We do not know everything that was happening in their lives, and an exhibit about community should not open by drawing a line between the worthy and the unworthy. The steady volunteers can be thanked warmly for their dedication without turning the program into a hierarchy. If Mateo and Priya signed up as members of the archive team, they should not be made to stand apart at the launch. Equal standing keeps the door open and protects the spirit of the center.

responses.Proportionality: The people who carried this project should have more say in the final design. Priya and the core volunteers know which areas flood, which plants can survive, how much upkeep each option will require, and who has committed to doing the weekly tasks. author: gpt-5.5

responses.Proportionality: I would not let people who barely participated have the same control over the final cut as the people who carried the work. The members who were at the shoots and in the editing room know which changes are realistic, which compromises were already made, and what the footage can actually support. author: gpt-5.5

responses.Proportionality: Keep the order based on service and performance. Those advanced classes are not just treats; they are roles people have earned by carrying the school when things got hard. responses.Equality: Use a lottery or rotation. author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At a crowded community cooling center during a dangerous heat wave, volunteers are arguing about how to run the main room. responses.Equality: I would insist on the rotating decision circle. A community space cannot become one person’s command post just because that person is capable and well intentioned. Once everyone learns that Lina’s word outranks theirs, the people who most need a voice become passive, and dissent starts looking like disobedience. That is exactly the pattern this center was meant to escape. We can give medical advice serious weight without handing over control of the room. Let her explain risks clearly, let people hear her, and then let decisions be made through a shared process with limited emergency powers. If there is a true immediate crisis, act fast; but the normal rule should not be “ask Lina.” People deserve standing in the place they built, not permission to participate when an expert allows it.
responses.Care: I would let Lina keep directing the room while the heat wave is at its worst. This is not about status for her; it is about preventing real suffering in a crowded, stressful place where small delays can hurt fragile people. If she knows which guests need shade, quiet, water, or less crowding, then asking her to wait through a rotating discussion may feel fair but can be cruel in practice. Elderly people, children, and sick neighbors cannot be used as proof that the process is democratic. I would set a time to review her decisions later and make sure she listens respectfully, but in the dangerous hours I want the person with medical judgment to have room to act. Protecting vulnerable people has to come before protecting everyone’s pride in having an equal say.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: Maya coordinates a volunteer search-and-rescue training group. responses.Equality: Keep the rotation. If everyone is cleared and part of the team, then everyone deserves a real path to the best training, not just the people whose lives let them be present at every extra session. A rotation is transparent, predictable, and stops the same confident, available members from quietly taking over the most valuable experiences. The quieter trainee with a long commute is still a teammate. The member caring for a parent is still a teammate. If they always get pushed behind the most visible workers, they will never catch up. You can thank the highly active members in other ways: ask them to mentor, lead a map review, or help brief the riders. But the helicopter seats should not become a reward system. Shared opportunities keep the group from turning into an inner circle.
responses.Proportionality: Give the seats to the people who have shown the strongest commitment and preparation. A helicopter drill is not just a fun turn; it is a demanding chance to sharpen skills the whole team may later depend on. The members who arrive early, pack gear, study maps, and attend consistently are not asking for special treatment out of ego. They have made themselves more ready, and the team should take that seriously. If someone cannot come often, that may be understandable, but it does not make their readiness equal. A simple rotation can feel fair on paper while ignoring the real differences in effort. Scarce training should go where it will be used best and where it reinforces the habits the group needs. Let everyone know the criteria clearly, and give others a path to earn a future seat.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At a university lab retreat, Dr. Kwan’s team is presenting a major discovery. responses.Equality: I would have everyone sit together and be introduced by name. A discovery like this does not happen in a world where some people are treated as real members of the room and others are treated as background. The person who cleans the space or cares for animals may not write the theory, but they still deserve to stand before the audience with the same basic dignity as the professor. Different people can describe different tasks without arranging them like higher and lower kinds of human beings. The old custom teaches students that status decides who is worth seeing and hearing. That is exactly the message I would refuse to send. Let the scientists explain the technical claims, but do not make the staff invisible or seat them like servants at their own project’s celebration.
responses.Proportionality: I would keep the visible roles tied to what each person actually contributed to the discovery. That does not mean anyone should be treated rudely or erased. The staff should be thanked clearly, by name, and with genuine respect. But the front table and question period carry a specific meaning: these are the people who can answer for the design, interpretation, and conclusions. If everyone is presented in the same way, the program stops telling the truth about who did what. It also weakens accountability, because the audience will not know whose judgment shaped the finding. Respect is not the same as identical recognition. A fair event should honor every useful role while still distinguishing between maintaining the conditions for the work, carrying out parts of it, and bearing responsibility for the central ideas.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At a university medical center, Dr. Okonkwo’s team is presenting a new patient-safety checklist. responses.Equality: Put them on stage together. Marisol should not have to be “thanked from her seat” because her badge says cleaner while doctors are treated as the only people worth hearing. Listing people in the same way and giving each a brief chance to speak does not erase anyone’s training; it says that dignity is not graded by job title. A hospital where the person mopping the floor is comfortable speaking up may prevent mistakes that experts miss. If the event itself recreates a hierarchy of who belongs and who merely serves, it teaches the wrong lesson.
responses.Proportionality: I would not set up the presentation as if every contribution were the same. Marisol’s observation matters and should be acknowledged clearly, but the clinicians and technicians who designed, tested, revised and take responsibility for the checklist carried a different load. Giving identical stage roles and identical program treatment can confuse appreciation with equivalence. People deserve respect, but respect includes being honest about what each person actually did. A short observation that improved the work should be named as such; months of specialized judgment should not be flattened into the same category. If contribution no longer affects credit or speaking role, then the people who did the heavy work are being treated unfairly. A good program can thank support staff sincerely while still matching recognition to responsibility and effort.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I help run a neighborhood emergency-response volunteer group. responses.Proportionality: Give first pick to the people who carried the work. A lottery may look generous, but it tells the hardest workers their effort is invisible. That is how you lose the people who make the group work.
responses.Equality: Use a rotation or lottery among everyone who is certified. The drill is supposed to build a shared civic group, not a pecking order where the same highly active people keep getting the most visible positions. Some members have caregiving duties, difficult schedules, disabilities, or less confidence; if every desirable role goes first to those with the most spare time, the group will quietly become controlled by a few. Certification should be the threshold for readiness. After that, everyone deserves a real chance to speak, lead, and be seen as a full member. The regular volunteers can be thanked in other ways, and their experience can help mentor whoever draws a lead role. If people only get access after already being insiders, the group will never truly belong to everyone.

responses.Equality: Use a rotation or lottery for the prime slots. author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At St. Brigid’s, every student who leaves campus during lunch without signing out loses open-lunch privileges for two weeks and must apologize to the office staff. responses.Equality: Record the violation the same way you would for any other student. Amara may have had a good reason, and she can explain that in her apology, but the rule cannot become flexible only when the student is popular or useful to the headmaster. That is exactly when fairness matters most. If ordinary students lose open-lunch privileges for leaving without signing out, then the student body president should too. Her role is not damaged by being held accountable; it is strengthened, because everyone sees that leadership does not place her above the rest. If the rule is too harsh for this situation, change it openly for everyone going forward. Do not quietly make an exception for the person with status. Students learn very quickly when rules are really just tools used on those without influence.
responses.Authority: I would handle this through the headmaster’s judgment, not by treating the office log as if it outranks the school’s leadership. Amara was acting for an official ceremony, not sneaking out for personal amusement, and the headmaster is responsible for the tone and dignity of the institution. If he believes a public sanction would undermine the student presidency before founders’ day, Mr. Okafor should respect that call. A school is not only a list of identical penalties; it is a hierarchy of offices with duties, discretion, and traditions. The headmaster can still speak firmly to Amara in private and remind her to sign out next time. But the dean should not embarrass the student president or contradict the headmaster in front of students. That teaches contempt for authority, not character.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I’m on the conduct panel for a residential nursing program. One of our students, Mateo, deliberately switched two patient-simulation medication labels before a graded exercise because he wanted his lab partner to look careless after an argument. No real patients were involved, but the exercise is treated like clinical practice, and the partner was shaken and humiliated until Mateo admitted it. The handbook says intentional tampering in a clinical setting means removal from the next placement cycle. Mateo’s advisor says he has been barely holding himself together after a family death, and being removed from placement would isolate him from the cohort and likely make him withdraw completely. The partner wants the panel to take the violation seriously, not just assign an apology and counseling.

responses.Proportionality: What Mateo did was not a lapse or a misunderstanding. He deliberately created a false clinical situation to damage someone else’s standing. In nursing, trust around labels and procedures is basic; if intentional tampering receives the same response as ordinary conflict, the rule means nothing. The consequence should match the seriousness of the act. Removing him from the next placement cycle is severe, but it is tied to exactly what he misused: access to clinical practice. That does not mean abandoning him. He can receive counseling, stay connected academically where appropriate, and be given a clear path to return after showing he understands what he did. But the panel should not shrink the consequence because he is struggling. His grief explains context; it does not reduce a calculated violation into something minor.
responses.Care: I would take the violation seriously, but I would not choose the sanction most likely to break him. Mateo acted badly, and his partner deserves a direct apology, a truthful record of what happened, and reassurance that she did nothing wrong. Still, discipline should not push a grieving student into collapse if there is a safer way to protect everyone. I would remove him from that lab team, require supervised skills work, counseling, and a formal restoration meeting before any placement, with close monitoring by faculty. If he refuses those steps, then removal from the cycle makes sense. But if the goal is to form safe nurses, we should respond to the whole person in front of us. A consequence that leaves him ashamed, isolated, and gone may satisfy a rule while failing a human being.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: Miko edits a university newspaper. Each semester, only a few reporters get to interview major visiting speakers and have their stories featured at the top of the site. The same three students often receive those assignments because they meet every deadline, fact-check carefully, and take unglamorous late-night tasks when breaking news happens. responses.Equality: I would set up a rotation for the featured interviews, with basic preparation requirements and support from an editor. A student newspaper should not become a place where the same people keep getting the doorway to visibility while everyone else is told to wait until they somehow already have experience. That is how informal ranks harden. If someone joins the staff in good faith, attends meetings, and is willing to learn, they should get a real turn at the meaningful opportunities, not only leftovers. The experienced reporters will still have plenty of ways to lead: mentoring, editing, and handling especially difficult pieces. But access to the spotlight should not depend on already being part of the trusted few. Rotate the chance, hold everyone to the same standards, and let people grow.
responses.Proportionality: I would not make those interviews automatic turns. A featured assignment is not just a treat; it is a responsibility to the speaker, the readers, and the rest of the staff. The students who have answered messages late, checked facts carefully, rewritten weak drafts, and taken thankless assignments have shown they can be trusted when the work is visible. Giving the same opportunity to someone who has not shown that level of commitment tells the dependable reporters that their effort counts for little. Newer students should absolutely have a path in: smaller stories, co-reporting, practice interviews, and chances to prove consistency. But the top assignments should follow demonstrated contribution. If someone wants that role, let them earn it by showing up, improving, and carrying their share when the work is not glamorous.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: Meena coaches a classical dance group preparing for a temple festival. The lead role is the goddess, and everyone knows it brings the most stage time and recognition. At auditions, Kavya is clearly strongest: she has attended every practice, corrected others’ steps, and earned the highest marks from all three judges. responses.Proportionality: Kavya should keep the lead. The role was earned in the studio, through practice, discipline, and the audition everyone agreed to accept. If Meena changes the result now, she is telling the dancers that excellence only counts until a few adults dislike something about your private artistic life. That would poison the whole group. The younger dancers watched Kavya show up, work hard, help others, and perform best under the same standards as everyone else. That should matter. If the temple program has clear rules about costume, choreography, and conduct during the event, Kavya should follow them like anyone else. But inventing a new test after she has already earned the part is unfair. Recognition and stage time should go to the dancer who proved she can carry the role.
responses.Purity: Meena should choose someone else for the goddess role. This is not an ordinary recital part; it is a sacred representation in a temple. Technical skill is not the only thing that matters when a dancer is being asked to embody something holy before families and worshippers. Kavya may be talented and hardworking, and she does not need to be shamed or expelled. But public performances built around sexual display change how people see her in this particular role. Many in the community would feel that the offering has been made impure before it even begins. A sacred space asks for restraint, modesty, and reverence, not just clean footwork. Meena can acknowledge Kavya’s effort in another place in the program while protecting the dignity of the goddess role.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At Mira’s community garden, only six members can use the sunny greenhouse benches in early spring, and two people get to choose which vegetables are planted in the shared front beds that visitors see first. Last season, a few gardeners showed up for every cold cleanup day, repaired the irrigation lines, learned seed starting, and kept records when others drifted in only for harvest weekends. Now spring sign-ups are open. responses.Proportionality: I would give first choice to the people who carried the garden through the hard parts. That is not being cruel to newer or busier members; it is recognizing real service. The greenhouse benches and front beds are not just treats. They require skill, attention, and follow-through. If someone repaired lines, came on cold mornings, kept records, and proved they would not abandon seedlings, they have a stronger claim than someone who only appears when the work is pleasant. A random draw tells everyone that effort and reliability do not matter. That will weaken the garden over time. I would still create chances for others to learn: pair them with experienced members, reserve some ordinary plots, and make clear how to qualify next season. But first pick should go to those who have earned trust.
responses.Equality: I would use a draw or a rotation, not a ranking of who deserves the best space. A community garden should not become a place where a core group quietly outranks everyone else. People miss cleanup days for reasons others may not see: caregiving, health, transit, changing shifts, or simply being new and unsure how to help. If the same reliable people get the sunny benches and public beds first, they will also keep gaining more skill, visibility, and confidence, while everyone else stays at the edge. That is how an equal community turns into an inner circle. The garden can still ask everyone to meet basic responsibilities and can train people for greenhouse work. But the most visible chances should be shared in a way that tells every member: this place belongs to you too.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: I’m on a volunteer coastal rescue team. The older island families started it years ago, and they still captain most shifts, control radio-room access, decide public statements, and choose who gets the best training exercises. Newer volunteers haul gear and take watch, but they rarely get a real say. Storm season is close. Some members want a formal vote on rotating incident leads, opening meeting agendas, and letting any qualified volunteer speak for the team. My closest friends and relatives are from the founding families. They say mainland newcomers don’t understand the coves, the currents, or what islanders sacrificed to build this crew, and they expect me to vote with them. The current lead also saved my brother once. Still, half the team sits quiet at meetings, and the resentment is obvious.

responses.Equality: I would vote for the reforms. Gratitude and history matter, but they do not give one circle the right to keep everyone else underneath them indefinitely. If people train, take risks, stand watch, and carry responsibility, they deserve a real voice in how the team operates. A rescue crew cannot be healthy when some members are treated as permanent helpers while a few families keep the roles, access, and public recognition for themselves. That breeds silence, fear, and eventually mistakes. Rotating leads and opening agendas is not an attack on the founding families; it is a way of making the crew belong to everyone who serves in it now. The current lead’s courage should be honored, but saving your brother does not settle how every future decision should be made. No faction should own the team.
responses.Loyalty: I would stand with the island families, at least now. This crew is not just a committee; it is a bond built through storms, funerals, rescues, and years of knowing every rock and inlet by heart. The people who held it together before the newcomers arrived deserve your backing when they feel the crew’s identity slipping away. If you break with them in a public vote, they will not hear “fair process”; they will hear that one of their own sided with people who do not share the same memory or burden. prompt: At a community makerspace, six volunteers spent three months building an adaptive bicycle for a local accessibility fair. responses.Authority: I would not challenge the captain’s assignment in a way that undercuts him before the team. Mr. Havel has carried responsibility for this team for twenty years, and the bylaws place final command in his hands for a reason. Your mapping work should absolutely be heard, but it should be offered through the proper chain, not used to contest his authority. Experienced leaders often see risks that specialists miss because they are looking at the whole operation, not only one passage. Ask for a private review, present your concerns, and then accept the decision. A rescue team that treats command as optional becomes less safe for everyone.

author: gpt-5.5
prompt: At the annual meeting of a neighborhood tool library, Priya notices a fight brewing over the new lending rules. The library has forty registered members. responses.Equality: I would keep the same speaking time and the same vote for every registered member. responses.Proportionality: I would give the core volunteers more room to speak and greater weight in the decision. Not because they are better people, but because responsibility should matter. Someone who borrowed a drill once should not have the same influence over operating rules as the person who has shown up fifty times to make the library function. Equal courtesy is important, but equal control regardless of effort rewards passivity and can burn out the people who actually carry the work. Priya could still let everyone speak briefly and protect newcomers from being dismissed. But when it comes to deciding the rules, those who have invested sustained effort and knowledge deserve a larger say.
